abstract: Logics of definitions extend first order intuitionistic logic with fixed-point definitions which associate formulas to atomic predicates. These associated formulas must be constrained for consistency. In the original formulation, predicate symbols were required to be ordered and only predicates lower in the order were allowed to appear negatively in the defining formula. This constraint renders ineligible definitions such as those of logical relations in which the predicate being defined must be allowed to appear negatively, albeit with smaller arguments. Tiu has formalized a weaker constraint called ground stratification that permits such definitions and has shown that it suffices for consistency. Definitions can also be given a least fixed-point interpretation via a special induction rule. We address the question of whether Tiu’s relaxation carries over to such a treatment. We propose a new induction rule for ground stratified inductive definitions that takes into account the fact that the definition of the predicate in question must itself be considered to be stratified by the complexity of its arguments to obtain a least fixed-point interpretation. We establish the consistency of the resulting logic and we illustrate its new capabilities via an example that encodes a strong normalizability proof for the simply typed λ-calculus in which the reducibility predicate is inductively defined by recursion on its arguments.

      Abstract
Logics of definitions extend first order intuitionistic logic with fixed-point definitions which associate
formulas to atomic predicates. These associated formulas must be constrained for consistency. In the
original formulation, predicate symbols were required to be ordered and only predicates lower in the
order were allowed to appear negatively in the defining formula. This constraint renders ineligible
definitions such as those of logical relations in which the predicate being defined must be allowed to
appear negatively, albeit with smaller arguments. Tiu has formalized a weaker constraint called
ground stratification that permits such definitions and has shown that it suffices for consistency.
Definitions can also be given a least fixed-point interpretation via a special induction rule. We
address the question of whether Tiu’s relaxation carries over to such a treatment. We propose
a new induction rule for ground stratified inductive definitions that takes into account the fact
that the definition of the predicate in question must itself be considered to be stratified by the
complexity of its arguments to obtain a least fixed-point interpretation. We establish the consistency
of the resulting logic and we illustrate its new capabilities via an example that encodes a strong
normalizability proof for the simply typed λ-calculus in which the reducibility predicate is inductively
defined by recursion on its arguments.

 1      Introduction
Logics of definitions, originally introduced by McDowell and Miller [14], extend conventional
predicate logics with the capability of treating predicate constants as defined symbols.
Formally, this treatment is realized by associating formulas with predicate constants through
a collection of clauses and including rules for using these clauses to “introduce” atomic
formulas in the course of derivations. In the simplest form, the rules build in a fixed-point
treatment of the definitions of predicates that are provided in this manner. However, as
shown by [17], the inference rules can be refined to yield a least or greatest fixed-point
interpretation to the definitions, thereby yielding capabilities for inductive and co-inductive
reasoning in the logic. The resulting logics are well-suited to encoding reasoning about
rule-based relational specifications, as has been amply established by experience with the
proof assistant Abella [2] that implements a particular variant called G [7].
    The definitions that are associated with predicate constants in the logics under considera-
tion must be constrained in order to ensure their consistency. Specifically, a definition must
not be circular in that it assumes its own existence in its construction. This requirement
translates concretely into restrictions on the negative occurrences of the predicate constant
in the formula defining it. The condition imposed in [14] is that there must be an ordering
on predicate constants that determines which of them have been already defined and can

       about properties of programming languages. The definition of these relations are typically

           In past work [11, 18], it has been shown that the restriction on fixed-point definitions can
       be weakened to a form that allows for building in of the arguments of an atomic formula into
       the stratification ordering while maintaining the stricter form of stratification for inductive
       definitions. The weaker condition has been called ground stratification. While this relaxation
       suffices for many applications, there are still some situations in which a ground stratified
       definition is required to be inductive.1 Whether such a capability can be coherently supported
       is the issue we take up here. Our results in this context are threefold. First, we show that we
       can sensibly provide a least fixed-point reading to a ground stratified fixed-point definition
       but that, to do so, we must think in terms of ground (variable-free) instances of the defining
       clauses. Second, we show that the logic can be endowed with inference rules for these
       definitions that approximate their understanding in this manner while retaining consistency.
       An important aspect of our additions is that they preserve the earlier treatment of inductive
       definitions under the stricter stratification condition. Finally, we demonstrate that there is
       practical utility to the augmentation to the logic that results from our work.
           The rest of the paper is organized as follows. The next section introduces the logic of fixed-
       point definitions. Section 3 discusses induction within this setting, culminating with inference
       rules for treating ground-stratified inductive definitions. The next two sections establish
       the consistency of the resulting logic and illustrate the usefulness of its new capabilities in
       formalizing a particular proof of strong normalizability for the simply typed lambda calculus.
       We conclude the paper with a discussion of related and future work. The paper includes
       two appendices, one of which elaborates on a discussion of least-fixed points associated
       with ground stratified inductive definitions and the other of which illustrates the use of
       ground-stratified inductive definitions in a proof of strong normalizability for System T.
       Formalizations of the examples in the paper within the Abella proof assistant are included
       as supplementary material.

       3.1      Strictly Stratified Definitions and Least Fixed-Points
       Fixed-point definitions can sometimes have multiple interpretations. To illustrate this
       possibility assume that the signature Σ identifies a propositional symbol p and then let D
       be a fixed-point definition comprising the sole clause p ≡∅ p. This definition is consistent
       with two different interpretations for p, one in which it does not hold and another in which
       it does; these correspond, respectively, to the least and greatest fixed-points associated with
       the definition. If we were to pick the least fixed-point, then we should be able to show that
       the sequent · : · ⊢ p ⊃ ⊥ holds. However, the logic does not build in that choice and this
       sequent is therefore not provable.

the strict stratification restriction. Towards this end, we first discuss how such definitions

         6     Conclusion

        In this paper, we have shown how to interpret ground stratified fixed-point definitions as
        inductive definitions. First, we have observed that we can make sense of such definitions
        as a family of inductive definitions identified by recursion on the level of the arguments of
        the predicate being defined. We have then introduced an induction rule via a new operator
        which approximates the infinitary interpretation of ground stratified inductive definitions
        as a family of least fixed-points and we have proved that the logic that includes this rule is
        consistent. The resulting logic subsumes the logic described in [11] that permitted only those
        inductive definitions that satisfied a stricter stratification condition. Finally, we have shown
        that the new rule allows us to encode a reducibility predicate that needs to be interpreted
        inductively, providing a new way of encoding strong normalizability proofs.
            As we have noted already, the work in this paper as well as in [11] has built on that
        of Tiu in [18]. Another related effort is that of Baelde and Nadathur [3], which extended
        the deduction modulo framework of Dowek and Werner [5] with inductive and co-inductive
        definitions that are stratified by an ordering that is dependent only on the predicate name. A
        counterpart to this idea in the setting of type theory has also been developed by Jacob-Rao
        et al. [12]. In the logic called µNJ that is described in [3], rewrite rules can be used to realize
        fixed-point definitions with a flexibility that overlaps significantly with what is supported by
        ground stratification. Thus, µNJ provides capabilities that are akin to those supported by
        the logic described in [11] and this work extends them in similar ways. Another effort that is
        important to mention is that of Van den Eede et al. [19]. On the surface, the motivation and
        approach for this work is similar to ours: it too wants to ease the stratification restriction for
        inductive definitions, and it does this by introducing a proof rule like ours for introducing
        atomic formulas that appear as assumptions and that are defined inductively. However, the
        logics that are considered in the two cases are different. Van den Eede et al. work within
        a classical logic and they use the well-founded semantics from logic programming [20] in
        interpreting definitions. In contrast, we have worked within an intuitionistic logic, and our
        treatment of definitions and, consequently, our consistency arguments are entirely proof-
